question.value: Investigate the impact of vertical thermal stratification on the azimuthal velocity of protoplanetary disks and determine whether a stratified model can explain velocity differences between CO isotopologues.

evidence.quote: We investigate the impact of thermal stratification on the azimuthal velocity of protoplanetary disks. The aim of this work is to determine whether a stratified model can explain this discrepancy.

claims.hypothesis: A vertically thermally stratified hydrostatic disk model accurately describes the density and azimuthal velocity fields of a stratified protoplanetary disk.
claims.experiment: Derive the analytical density and rotation curve equations for a thermally stratified disk and compare them against 3D SPH simulations of a stratified disk (MWC 480 setup) using phantom.
claims.result: At z = 20 au after eight outer orbits, the sub-Keplerian deviation (v_k^2 - v_phi^2)/v_k^2 reaches 10-12% and is matched by the stratified model, whereas the isothermal model fails to reproduce the density and velocity profiles.
claims.finding: The analytical thermally stratified model accurately describes the simulated density and velocity fields and is a major improvement over the vertically isothermal model.

evidence.quote: The stratified model perfectly describes the density and the velocity field of the simulation and is a significant improvement over the isothermal one.

In particular, in the right panel of Fig. 1, we can see that the difference between the azimuthal velocity and the Keplerian velocity ( v [2] k [−] [v] [2] ϕ [)/] [v] k [2] [reaches the 10] [−] [12% and] only the stratified model is able to reproduce it.

claims.hypothesis: Vertical thermal stratification can explain the observed velocity differences between 12CO and 13CO rotation curves in MAPS protoplanetary disks and improve dynamical estimates of star mass, disk mass, and scale radius.
claims.experiment: Simultaneously fit 12CO and 13CO rotation curves of the five MAPS disks using both vertically isothermal and thermally stratified self-gravitating models.
claims.result: The reduced chi-squared decreases for all five disks when using the stratified model (e.g., from 90.84 to 8.48 in GM Aur and from 35.68 to 6.29 in IM Lup), and best-fit scale radii increase from 38-80 au to more realistic values of 91-128 au.
claims.finding: Thermal stratification reconciles most of the velocity inconsistencies between 12CO and 13CO and provides more realistic stellar masses, disk masses, and scale radii, though localized deviations remain in the outer disk of IM Lup, substructured regions of HD 163296, and the compact inner disk of AS 209.

evidence.quote: When thermal stratification is taken into account, it is possible to reconcile most of the inconsistencies between rotation curves of different isotopologues.

claims.hypothesis: Dynamical disk masses derived from thermally stratified rotation curve models yield standard gas-to-dust ratios and indicate whether the MAPS disks are gravitationally unstable.
claims.experiment: Combine the stratified-model disk gas masses with optically thin 283 GHz dust masses to compute gas-to-dust ratios, and evaluate radial Toomre Q profiles.
claims.result: Inferred gas-to-dust ratios range between 108 and 240 (< 192 for AS 209), and Toomre Q is greater than 1 everywhere, with minimum values of ~4 in GM Aur and ~6 in IM Lup.
claims.finding: The gas-to-dust ratios are within a factor of ~2 of the standard value of 100, and all disks are gravitationally stable according to Q > 1, though spiral-hosting disks (GM Aur and IM Lup) are closer to the instability regime.
